summary: Gives guidance on selecting labels for DNS-Based Service Discovery when it is used with conventional DNS and other name resolution systems. DNS-SD can use full DNS capability, and environments differ in their treatment of IDNA and UTF-8 labels.

eli5.summary: When you name something so friends from different countries can find it, you need to pick letters everyone can handle.

subtitle: How to choose names that work across DNS and mDNS without confusion.

tldr.problem: DNS-Based Service Discovery (DNS-SD) can use either conventional DNS or other systems like Multicast DNS (mDNS). DNS uses strict naming rules (LDH: letters, digits, hyphens) and enforces IDNA for international names, while mDNS allows any UTF-8 characters. When the same names need to work in both systems, confusion and failures result.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC outlines requirements for label selection based on which parts of a service name go through DNS resolution. The Instance portion (the user-visible service name) is exempted and can use any UTF-8. The Domain portion must follow DNS conventions. The Service portion uses special underscore labels that DNS resolvers must already handle.
tldr.outcome: Applications can design DNS-SD implementations that handle each name portion correctly, allowing names to work reliably whether they are resolved through DNS or mDNS without requiring system-wide IDNA processing to break the service name apart.

facts.label: mDNS encoding
facts.value: UTF-8 with spaces and Unicode allowed

facts.label: IDNA processing
facts.value: Converts U-labels to A-labels for international domains

today: RFC 8222 is Informational and provides guidance for DNS-SD implementations, not a normative standard. It remains current as guidance for handling the enduring tension between DNS's strict naming conventions and the flexibility of local-network systems like mDNS.

sections.title: Service Discovery Across Systems
sections.content:
DNS-Based Service Discovery (DNS-SD) is a mechanism for discovering services using queries to DNS or other systems like Multicast DNS (mDNS). Despite its name, DNS-SD works with any system that understands domain names, not just DNS itself.

The problem is that different naming systems have different rules. The traditional DNS system only allows letters, digits, and hyphens in labels (the LDH rule). For international characters, DNS uses IDNA, which converts Unicode characters to special ASCII representations. By contrast, mDNS (which runs on local networks without centralized servers) requires UTF-8 encoding and allows almost any Unicode character, including spaces and punctuation.

When users want to use the same service names in both DNS and mDNS environments—or when a name might be resolved by either system depending on context—these conflicting conventions create problems. A name that works perfectly in mDNS might fail in DNS, and vice versa.
sections.eli5: Imagine two post offices with different rules about what goes on an address label. One only accepts letters and numbers. The other accepts almost anything, including pictures and emoji. When you send mail that needs to work at both, you have to be careful about the format.

sections.title: Naming Conventions and Their Limits
sections.content:
The LDH rule (letters, digits, hyphen) was never a hard requirement of DNS itself. It is merely a convention, established because many early applications assumed this pattern. The Internationalized Domain Names for Applications (IDNA) standards were developed to handle Unicode in DNS, but they layer additional constraints on top of LDH.

IDNA conversion (called U-label to A-label transformation) happens automatically in some system libraries. However, this automatic conversion is context-unaware: a library converting the entire domain name may incorrectly process part of a DNS-SD name that should remain in UTF-8 form. Furthermore, the infrastructure zones (top-level domains, the root) publish only IDNA-compatible forms, never raw UTF-8.

Multicast DNS, on the other hand, requires UTF-8 labels and explicitly encourages spaces, punctuation, and a broad range of Unicode. A typical mDNS service might be named "My Printer" with a space, which DNS would reject outright.
sections.eli5: DNS started with simple rules (letters and numbers only) and added IDNA to handle other languages. mDNS said "anything goes" and uses UTF-8 directly. When one system automatically converts your name using IDNA, it might break the parts that should stay as simple UTF-8.

sections.title: Requirements for Label Interoperation
sections.content:
For DNS-SD to work reliably across these systems, a service name must be carefully constructed. A DNS-SD Service Instance Name has three portions: <Instance> (the human-visible service name), <Service> (metadata like "_http._tcp"), and <Domain> (the zone the service is in).

Different portions face different pressures. The <Service> portion uses underscore-prefixed labels that are already special in DNS (used for DNS SRV records). System-wide resolvers that cannot handle underscores will not work with DNS-SD at all, so there is no risk of accidental IDNA processing here. Underscores are formally incompatible with IDNA, so this portion requires no profile restrictions.

The <Instance> and <Domain> portions, however, may be subject to DNS resolution and IDNA processing. The strategy differs for each: <Instance> is user-facing and should allow rich Unicode, while <Domain> is part of the actual DNS lookup path and must interoperate with the public DNS infrastructure.
sections.eli5: A service name has three parts, and each one travels through the system in a different way. The metadata part (what kind of service) is safe because DNS already knows how to handle it. The human-readable name and the zone name need special care.

sections.title: The Instance Portion: User-Facing Flexibility
sections.content:
The <Instance> portion of a DNS-SD name is the user-visible string: "Bedroom Printer", "Dad's Music", or even emoji-containing names in local contexts. RFC 6763 is clear that virtually any character is permitted in the instance portion. Unlike general-purpose domain names, which users type into browsers, DNS-SD names are typically chosen from a list by the user, so there is no need to restrict characters for typability or confusion avoidance.

The wrong approach would be to apply the same profile restrictions to <Instance> that DNS requires, because that would eliminate the human-facing value of mDNS. Instead, DNS-SD implementations should intercept the <Instance> portion and ensure it is never handed to system-wide IDNA-aware resolvers that might mangle it.

The practical consequence is that DNS-SD software must use special-purpose name resolution code, not generic system resolvers, for the <Instance> portion. Zone operators who want to support DNS-SD must be prepared to accept labels with spaces, uppercase letters, and arbitrary UTF-8, and they should not apply the LDH rule to all labels.
sections.eli5: The user-visible name can be anything because users pick it from a list, not type it from memory. The trick is making sure the system does not try to convert it the way it would a regular domain name.

sections.title: The Domain Portion: DNS Compatibility
sections.content:
The <Domain> portion of a DNS-SD name forms part of the owner name submitted to DNS resolution. A system-wide IDNA-aware resolver will interpret UTF-8 labels in the owner name as candidates for IDNA processing. More importantly, operators of internationalized domains publish them in the public DNS as A-labels (the IDNA-encoded form); the topmost labels are always A-labels.

Therefore, the <Domain> portion must be subject to a profile that prioritizes IDNA-compatible labels. DNS-SD implementations should identify the <Domain> portion and treat it subject to IDNA2008 when the domain is to be queried from the global DNS. If resolution fails, an implementation may attempt fallback by substituting plain UTF-8 labels from the lowest level upward, but it should not try UTF-8 first because that would generate unnecessary traffic to the public DNS infrastructure.

Some zone operators might support both a UTF-8 version and an IDNA version of their zones using DNAME records or parallel delegations, but this introduces fragility and requires coordination between different departments. The recommended approach is for resolvers to be aware of zone boundaries and adapt their preference based on whether a lookup is below or above the organizational boundary of the DNS tree.
sections.eli5: The zone name (the part that is actually looked up in DNS) has to follow DNS rules because the public DNS infrastructure uses IDNA. Try the DNS-friendly way first, and only if that fails should you try plain UTF-8.
